# Introduction

Metaproteomes are usually compared by accession: Bray-Curtis, or a test per
protein, treats two different proteins as unrelated even when they share fold
and function. Proteins of one function in different organisms are often too
far apart in sequence for a sequence clustering to join them. `repdist`
compares proteins by their embeddings from a protein language model, by
default TM-Vec, where the cosine similarity of two proteins is their
predicted TM-score. On that representation it

- measures **beta diversity**: `sample_mmd()` gives a sample-by-sample
    distance, the maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) between the samples'
    abundance-weighted distributions over the embeddings;
- **bins proteins**: `protein_similarity()` and `bin_proteins()` group
    structurally similar proteins by Markov clustering;
- feeds **differential abundance**: `bin_glom()` sums counts within bins.

The goal is to see a change in what the proteins do, not only in which
accessions are present.

## The simulated data

`simulate_cog` is built from the NCBI COG 2024 release (Galperin et al. 2025)
so that the answer is known:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| Samples | 20: 10 in group A, 10 in group B |
| Background | 100 proteins from other COGs, in every sample |
| Treatment | 10 GrpE proteins (COG0576), one per group-A sample |
| Remote homology | each GrpE protein in its own MMseqs2 30%-identity cluster |
| Perturbation | 5% of each group-A sample's abundance on its GrpE protein |
| Counts | negative binomial, depth 20,000 |

Group A is enriched for one function, GrpE, but no protein and no sequence
family is enriched in more than one sample. `?simulate_cog` gives the
details, and `inst/scripts/make_simulate_cog.R` how it was built.

```{r install, eval = FALSE}
if (!requireNamespace("BiocManager", quietly = TRUE)) {
    install.packages("BiocManager")
}
# dependencies = TRUE also installs vegan and ggplot2, used below
BiocManager::install("repdist", dependencies = TRUE)
```

```{r libs}
library(repdist)
library(vegan)
library(ggplot2)
data(simulate_cog, package = "repdist")
samples <- simulate_cog$samples
annotation <- simulate_cog$annotation
```

# Protein embeddings

Everything starts from a FASTA file of the proteins identified in the
samples. `embed_proteins()` reads it and returns an `AAStringSet` with one
embedding per protein in `mcols(proteins)$embedding`. Its first call
downloads the model (up to a few GB), so it does not run here;
`simulate_cog` ships the result. Once the model is downloaded, the 110
proteins take about 40 seconds on a laptop with an Apple M-series GPU.
`known_models()` lists the models, and `read_fasta()` reads and checks a
FASTA file.

```{r embed, eval = FALSE}
fasta <- system.file("extdata", "simulate_cog.fasta", package = "repdist")
proteins <- embed_proteins(fasta) # model = "tmvec"
```

```{r proteins}
proteins <- simulate_cog$proteins
proteins
dim(S4Vectors::mcols(proteins)$embedding)
```

The names of `proteins` must match the column names of the count table.

# Beta diversity

The count table has samples in rows and proteins in columns. `sample_mmd()`
and Bray-Curtis both compare relative abundances.

```{r distances}
counts <- simulate_cog$counts
relative <- counts / rowSums(counts)
D <- list(MMD = sample_mmd(relative, proteins),
    `Bray-Curtis` = vegdist(relative, "bray"))
```

PERMANOVA (`adonis2()`) tests whether the groups differ, and PERMDISP
(`betadisper()`) whether they differ in spread, each with 999 permutations.

```{r permanova}
set.seed(1)
mmd <- adonis2(D$MMD ~ group, data = samples)
set.seed(1)
bc <- adonis2(D$`Bray-Curtis` ~ group, data = samples)
disp <- vapply(D, function(d) {
    set.seed(1)
    permutest(betadisper(d, samples$group))$tab[1, "Pr(>F)"]
}, numeric(1))
knitr::kable(data.frame(distance = names(D), R2 = c(mmd$R2[1], bc$R2[1]),
    p = c(mmd$`Pr(>F)`[1], bc$`Pr(>F)`[1]), PERMDISP_p = disp,
    row.names = NULL), digits = 3)
```

Group A is more spread out under both distances, as the design builds in:
each group-A sample carries a different GrpE protein, and no group-B sample
carries one.

Principal coordinates (`cmdscale()`); each group's outermost samples are
joined by a line (its convex hull).

```{r pcoa}
#| fig.width: 8
#| fig.height: 3.8
#| fig.alt: "PCoA of the samples under MMD and Bray-Curtis, group convex hulls"
pcoa <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(D), function(k) {
    data.frame(samples, cmdscale(D[[k]], k = 2), distance = k)
}))
pcoa$distance <- factor(pcoa$distance, names(D))
hull <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(pcoa, ~ distance + group), function(d) {
    d[chull(d$X1, d$X2), ]
}))
ggplot(pcoa, aes(X1, X2, colour = group)) +
    geom_point(size = 2) +
    geom_polygon(data = hull, fill = NA) +
    facet_wrap(~distance, scales = "free") +
    labs(x = "PCo1", y = "PCo2") +
    theme_bw()
```

MMD separates the groups and Bray-Curtis does not. Bray-Curtis compares
accessions, and each GrpE protein is in one sample only, so to it the
enrichment is noise; MMD credits the ten GrpE proteins for being close in
the embedding space.

# Protein bins and differential abundance

`protein_similarity()` joins two proteins when their alignment has an
E-value of at most 0.01, weighting the edge by their predicted TM-score.
`bin_proteins()` splits that graph by Markov clustering and returns each
protein's bin (`membership`), the proteins of each bin (`clusters`) and
each bin's medoid (`representatives`).

```{r bins}
# aligns every pair with a positive similarity: quadratic in proteins
S <- protein_similarity(proteins, progress = FALSE)
bins <- bin_proteins(S)
table(size = lengths(bins$clusters))
```

The GrpE labels were not used to build the bins, so they can score them:
coherence is the share of the GrpE proteins in the bin that holds most of
them, and purity the share of that bin's proteins that are GrpE.

```{r scores}
grpe <- annotation$protein[annotation$role == "GrpE"]
grpe_bin <- names(which.max(table(bins$membership[grpe])))
c(coherence = mean(bins$membership[grpe] == grpe_bin),
    purity = mean(bins$clusters[[grpe_bin]] %in% grpe))
```

`bin_glom()` sums the counts within each bin. Any differential abundance
method can take the bin table; here a linear model per bin on the centred
log-ratio (CLR) of the counts, with a pseudo count of 1, and
Benjamini-Hochberg adjustment. LFC is the log2 fold change of group A over
group B. Bins with p < 0.05:

```{r da}
bin_counts <- bin_glom(counts, bins) # samples x bins
clr <- log2(bin_counts + 1)
clr <- clr - rowMeans(clr)
group <- factor(samples$group, c("B", "A"))
fit <- t(apply(clr, 2, function(y) {
    summary(lm(y ~ group))$coefficients["groupA", c("Estimate", "Pr(>|t|)")]
}))
res <- data.frame(bin = rownames(fit), LFC = fit[, 1], p = fit[, 2],
    q = p.adjust(fit[, 2], "BH"))
res <- res[res$p < 0.05, ]
knitr::kable(transform(res, LFC = round(LFC, 2),
    p = formatC(p, format = "g", digits = 2),
    q = formatC(q, format = "g", digits = 2)),
    row.names = FALSE)
```

The GrpE bin, `r grpe_bin`, stands out, although each GrpE protein is
abundant in one sample only.

# Notes

`protein_similarity()` aligns every pair with a positive similarity and
`sample_mmd()` holds a protein-by-protein kernel, so on real data use the
proteins identified in
your samples, never a whole search database: 20,000 proteins take about 3 GB.
`protein_similarity()` parallelises with `n_cores`. Structural similarity
does not guarantee shared function: the GrpE bin also holds a DnaK protein,
GrpE's HSP-70 partner.
